lens: Fact and integrity audit of /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/essays/excavation-not-demolition.json against its claims ledger /home/user/livewell-land/docs/work/essays/ledgers/excavation-not-demolition.md, the BSB chapter files in client/public/bible/ch/, and the integrity rules in docs/work/essays/BRIEF.md. Read-only; 15 web searches run on 2026-10-28 (search-engine summaries only, no page opened).

findings.where: Where It Usually Starts, The Great Dechurching paragraph: "Jim Davis and Michael Graham, working with surveys run by the political scientists Ryan Burge and Paul Djupe, wrote *The Great Dechurching* (2023) about the millions of American adults who once went to church regularly and now almost never go."
findings.problem: Restoration (g). The ledger (first closing run, change 2) records the writer's original figure and the authors' definition, generalized only because no source had been seen. The second closing run then saw both (UnHerd, ChurchLeaders, WBUR, Equip.org, as summarized) but left them out. This run's search saw them again: ChurchLeaders' "What 40 Million Dechurched Americans Say About Why They Left", WBUR and the Equip.org review, as summarized, give about 40 million US adults and define a dechurched person as someone who used to go to church at least once per month but now goes less than once a year; the same summary confirms Davis and Graham worked with Ryan Burge and Paul Djupe. One summary notes the 40 million counts all faiths; the sentence attributes the estimate to the authors, so it stands as theirs.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Jim Davis and Michael Graham, working with surveys run by the political scientists Ryan Burge and Paul Djupe, estimated in *The Great Dechurching* (2023) that about 40 million American adults who once went to church at least monthly now go less than once a year." Update ledger line 137 and the second-closing-run summary (line 17) to say the figure was restored.

findings.where: What Deserves to Come Down, first paragraph: "built on a national survey of American teenagers and long interviews with some of them."
findings.problem: Restoration (g). The ledger (first closing run, change 3) records the writer's original "a national survey of more than three thousand American teenagers and long interviews with more than two hundred of them". The second closing run kept the general wording because two counts seemed to disagree (3,290 vs 3,370). This run's search reconciles them: the NSYR's baseline was a nationally representative telephone survey of 3,290 teenagers aged 13 to 17 and their parents, plus an oversample of 80 Jewish households, for 3,370 completed cases, and 267 in-person interviews (summary of religionlink.com, the Princeton DSS catalog entry and the NSYR's own news page). Either count is "more than three thousand"; 267 is "more than two hundred". The writer's rounded wording is confirmed on both readings.
findings.fix: Replace "built on a national survey of American teenagers and long interviews with some of them." with "built on a national survey of more than three thousand American teenagers and long interviews with more than two hundred of them." Update ledger line 145 and line 17.

findings.where: Where It Usually Starts, Guidepost paragraph: "found that staff of the Southern Baptist Convention's Executive Committee had for years kept a private list of ministers accused of sexual abuse"
findings.problem: Restoration (g). The ledger (first closing run, change 1) records the writer's "for more than a decade", generalized because no result had shown it; the second closing run says it was not seen. This run's search saw it: the summary of the AP story as carried by NBC affiliates, WABE/GPB, Religion News Service and bishop-accountability.org quotes the Guidepost report: "Despite collecting these reports for more than 10 years, there is no indication that (Oldham and Boto) or anyone else, took any action", and a Baptist Message / Baptist & Reflector summary says reports were submitted to Boto as early as 2007. The finding stays attributed to the investigation (Oldham disputes it, per Baptist Press; the essay names no one).
findings.fix: Replace "had for years kept a private list of ministers accused of sexual abuse" with "had for more than a decade kept a private list of ministers accused of sexual abuse". Update ledger line 127 and line 17.

findings.where: Opening paragraph, last sentence: "he wrote that his faith in Jesus had gone through a massive shift, and added: "The popular phrase for this is 'deconstruction,' the biblical phrase is 'falling away.'""
findings.problem: Restoration (g). Correction 1 in the ledger turned Harris's first sentence into paraphrase because it rested on memory; the closing run then saw it quoted by Fox 5 Atlanta and other Fox affiliates, and this run's search saw it again (summary of ChurchLeaders, Fox 29, KTVU, Fox 5 Atlanta: "I have undergone a massive shift in regard to my faith in Jesus," Harris wrote). Both sentences are now confirmed verbatim. Whether they sit side by side in the post was not printed in any summary (a search for the joined string returned the same Fox and ChurchLeaders pages, which suggests it but does not show it), so the restoration below keeps them as two quotations.
findings.fix: Replace with: "he wrote, "I have undergone a massive shift in regard to my faith in Jesus," and added: "The popular phrase for this is 'deconstruction,' the biblical phrase is 'falling away.'"" (If a page is opened that shows the two sentences adjacent, the writer's original single quotation can be used instead: he wrote: "I have undergone a massive shift in regard to my faith in Jesus. The popular phrase for this is 'deconstruction,' the biblical phrase is 'falling away.'") Update ledger lines 117 and 87.

findings.where: Opening paragraph: "Harris was still a young man when *I Kissed Dating Goodbye* came out in 1997"
findings.problem: Restoration (g). Correction 2 replaced the writer's "in his early twenties" because it rested on an unchecked birth year. The closing run then saw a bookseller's description and 2018 coverage saying he wrote the book at 21; this run's search summary shows ChurchLeaders and NPR saying he was 21 when he wrote it and Exodus Books giving a 1974 birth year. 21 or 22 in 1996-97 is "early twenties" on any reading.
findings.fix: Replace "Harris was still a young man when *I Kissed Dating Goodbye* came out in 1997" with "Harris was in his early twenties when *I Kissed Dating Goodbye* came out in 1997". Update ledger line 113.

findings.where: What Deserves to Come Down, first paragraph: "In 2005 the sociologist Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton published *Soul Searching*"
findings.problem: Restoration (g). Correction 3 changed the writer's "the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton" only because Denton's discipline was unverified. This run's search saw it: her University of Texas at San Antonio faculty profile and Springtide Research Institute bio, as summarized, list her as a professor of sociology at UTSA with a Ph.D. and M.A. in sociology from UNC-Chapel Hill and a co-investigator of the National Study of Youth and Religion. The singular also reads oddly, as if Denton's role were being withheld.
findings.fix: Replace "the sociologist Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton" with "the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton". Update ledger line 144 and correction 3.

findings.where: What Deserves to Come Down, first paragraph: "They gave the faith most of those teenagers actually held a name: moralistic therapeutic deism."
findings.problem: Mismatch (c) and a claim about living scholars (f). The ledger (line 146) has Smith and Denton calling it "the de facto dominant religion" among American teenagers. Smith's own statement, in his essay "On 'Moralistic Therapeutic Deism' as U.S. Teenagers' Actual, Tacit, De Facto Religious Faith" (catholiceducation.org summary in this run), offers it "somewhat tentatively, as less than a conclusive fact but more than mere conjecture": "we suggest that the de facto dominant religion among contemporary teenagers in the United States is what we might call 'Moralistic Therapeutic Deism.'" "Dominant" is not "most", and the essay drops the authors' own hedge, so it credits them with a stronger finding than they claimed.
findings.fix: Replace with: "They gave a name to what they suggested was the dominant faith among those teenagers: moralistic therapeutic deism." (No quotation marks needed; the following "Its creed, as they summarized it" still reads.) Update ledger line 146 to record the wording.

findings.where: Augustine Took His Faith Apart Too, first paragraph: "When their most famous teacher, Faustus, came to Carthage and could not answer his questions"
findings.problem: No ledger line (a) for the superlative. Ledger line 201 covers only Faustus coming to Carthage and failing to answer (Confessions 5.3, 5.7). Confessions calls him a Manichee bishop whose coming Augustine had awaited for almost nine years; this run's search summary (Wikipedia, "Faustus of Mileve"; First Things) says the same and calls him charming and eloquent, but no source seen calls him the sect's most famous teacher.
findings.fix: Replace "When their most famous teacher, Faustus, came to Carthage" with "When Faustus, a Manichee bishop he had waited years to meet, came to Carthage". Add a ledger line citing Confessions 5.6 ("for almost all those nine years") for the wait.

findings.where: Opening paragraph, "Now, days after announcing that he and his wife were separating, he wrote...", read together with Why Some Christians Are Worried: "Some deconstruction is a decision already made, out looking for respectable reasons. Pastors can tell you about people who found serious objections to the faith in the same season they found a reason to want out of it."
findings.problem: Possible unfairness to a living person (f). Each sentence is accurate (the separation and the post are verified, ledger line 116, and this run's search again showed the mid-July separation and the late-July post). But the only named deconstructor in the essay is introduced with his marriage ending days earlier, and a later paragraph describes people whose objections arrived "in the same season they found a reason to want out". A reader can join the two into an insinuation about Harris's motives that the essay elsewhere refuses ("it isn't ours to finish for him"). The separation does no work in the argument.
findings.fix: Cut the clause: "Now he wrote that his faith in Jesus had gone through a massive shift, and added: ..." (or, with the Harris restoration above, "Now he wrote, "I have undergone a massive shift in regard to my faith in Jesus," and added: ..."). Leave the later general sentence as it is. If James wants the chronology kept, no fact needs changing.

findings.fix: No essay change recommended. Record in ledger line 169 that the year is confirmed (Tyndale Momentum, October 2020). If James wants it, the restored text is "she describes in *Another Gospel?* (2020) how a class at her own church".
